design.note: Systematic review with a random-effects meta-analysis of one domain and narrative synthesis of the rest; the card says which parts are pooled and which are not.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: the text on p. 279 says the subcategory analyses showed both groups performing significantly more poorly, and all four Table 3 subtest intervals on p. 280 include zero.
Confirmed: the abstract (p. 273) and the Conclusion (p. 282) both state that longer abstinence did not bring greater improvement, and p. 279 states the analysis was not done.

Confirmed and recomputed. Text: 228, 218, 229 for five studies and 74, 51, 47 for the four-study verbal subset. Adding Taurah's 154, 157 and 182 to the subset gives 228, 208 and 229, so the abstinent total is 208, not 218. Table 2's four smaller studies sum to 87, 51 and 49, which also fails to match the text's 74 and 47.

Confirmed: Taurah's abstinent group 66% men and 24% women; Ward's current group 29% and 61% and comparison group 23% and 67%; Potter's abstinent group n = 17 but 4 men and 11 women with age 24.7 (2.5), identical to the Morgan et al. (2002) abstinent row.

Confirmed against Murphy et al. (2009), Table 2, which I read for the other card. Ung's own reference list has 2004a as the verbal working memory paper (Hum Psychopharmacol 19: 225-234) and 2004b as the visuospatial paper (Psychopharmacology 173: 391-397), while Table 2 attaches 25/10/18 and 655.58 tablets (the visuospatial study in Murphy) to the 2004a row and 42/17/31 and 552.99 (the verbal study in Murphy) to the 2004b row: the rows are swapped against the labels. Wareing et al. (2005) is 291.33 here and 591.33 in Murphy. Two further mismatches to add: the 2004b row carries SD 718.44, the same value as the 2005 row, where Murphy gives 681.49; and the Wareing et al. (2007) comparison group is aged 22.85 here and 22.58 in Murphy.
Confirmed: a 2-year study on p. 279, findings at 18 months on p. 280, minimum abstinence 24 months in Table 2.

Confirmed: the Discussion (pp. 281-282) credits Taurah et al. (2014) with executive-function impairment that did not improve over an average of 5 years, while Table 2 lists it as cross-sectional and assessing learning and memory and complex attention only, and it is not among the 10 executive-function studies.

Confirmed: p. 274 cites McCann et al. (1994) as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage, and that paper's HVA difference held only in women and not on unequal-variance testing (checked against the source, card sc_mccann_1994).

instrument.note: AMSTAR 2 for a systematic review with meta-analysis (METHODS 5.3); the item-specific responses follow the allowed vocabulary.

domains.item: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria

domains.note: Partial yes is right: an Open Science Framework protocol exists and is dated, but it was revised during the review and is not reproduced, so the pre-specification of outcomes cannot be checked.

No, strictly: six databases, a librarian-built strategy, reference lists, no language limit and a search within 24 months, but the restriction to peer-reviewed publications is not justified, which blocks even partial yes. A reader who treated peer review as an eligibility criterion rather than a publication restriction would reach partial yes; the overall rating does not turn on it.

8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Partial yes is generous given the Table 2 errors above, but the item asks about coverage, not accuracy, so it stands.

domains.note: No is right: unadjusted group means pooled from non-randomized studies with I2 of 80 to 96% and no exploration of the heterogeneity.

domains.item: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Yes is defensible on the single sensitivity analysis, though it covers only the current-versus-abstinent comparison.

domains.item: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported

overall.note: Critically low confidence: more than one critical item unmet (7, 11, 15 at least). The reasoning is right that this is a judgment about the pooled numbers, not about the question.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Two headline statements do not follow from the Results: that the verbal subtests showed significantly poorer performance (all four intervals include zero) and that longer abstinence brought no greater improvement (not tested). Both are in the abstract, which is what most readers will see.

missed: The four Wareing executive-function studies share the same abstinent participants (the card has this in key finding 7), so the ten executive-function studies rest on at most seven independent samples. The card does not carry that count forward, and METHODS 6.3 requires overlapping evidence to be stated wherever the claim counts studies. The seven case-control studies reported as finding no abstinent-versus-naive difference include those four.

The reason the review gives for not doing a dose-response analysis (p. 282: most participants would count as heavy users at more than 100 lifetime tablets) is worth recording beside the fact that it was not done, because it is also the reason the review cannot speak to lighter use.

Thomasius et al. (2006), the 2.5-year abstinence study quoted in the Discussion for possible transporter recovery without memory recovery, was excluded from the review itself for a washout shorter than 7 days in its current-use group (p. 281). The card cites the finding without that context, which matters because the study is used in the Discussion to carry an argument the review's own criteria kept out of the evidence base.

The review's own framing of its contribution ('to the authors' knowledge, has not specifically been studied before', p. 282) sits oddly with the five earlier meta-analyses it summarizes in the Introduction; not an error, but a reader comparing this card with the Murphy card will want the overlap noted.
